For example, a Montessori is a public or private school that implements the Montessori Method of Education. These unique schools are best known for the following elements:

  • Mixed-aged classrooms
  • Student choice of activity from within a prescribed range of options
  • Uninterrupted, hours-long blocks of work time.
  • Students that learn from working with materials, rather than from direct instruction
  • Specialized educational materials made from wood rather than plastic
  • Environments designed so that learning materials are organized, and within reach of the child; as opposed to being locked up or out-of-bounds
  • Free movement within the classroom
  • Teachers trained to observe each individual child's characteristics, tendencies, innate talents and abilities.

However, because the term "Montessori" is considered public domain, not all schools using this name should be considered true Montessori's. This is important to keep in mind; studies have shown that students attending a true Montessori outperform other students in "mathematics and science," while another found that the Montessori Method had some of the largest positive effects on achievement of all programs evaluated.

It's also interesting to learn that, because the Montessori Method was developed for children, not adolescents, middle and highschool methodologies are still being debated and created. Maria Montessori did not establish a teacher training program or a detailed plan of education for adolescents during her lifetime. However, she did note, "during the difficult time of adolescence it is helpful to leave the accustomed environment ... and to go to quiet surroundings." Based on this, a large number of schools for ages 12-18 are set in rural locations, close to nature.

--

There's also the Sudbury school, which has no curriculum or set of required courses. These schools are considered a form of "democratic education;" there are over 60 around the world, all sharing some common elements:

  • Students and teachers are treated as near-equals
  • Students decided for themselves what to do with their time, and are responsible for their own education
  • No classrooms; students can choose when and where to congregate
  • Mixed-aged
  • Parents have little or no involvement in the school administration
  • School decisions are voted on in School Meetings
  • No tests, evaluations, or transcripts

The Sudbury education model states that "learning is a process someone does, not a process that is done to him or her". Learning is self-initiated and self-motivated. Teachers are available, but their instruction or guidance is not required.

Most school decisions are made in School Meetings, through a democratic process in which students and teachers have an equal vote. These Meetings are used to pass, amend, and repeal school rules; manage the school budget; make hiring and firing decisions; and make decisions regarding the suspension and expulsion of other students.

This Model places a lot of value on gaining experience; noting that children are capable of guiding themselves, and are apt at developing the skills needed to function as adults on their own.

--

Parochial schools are private schools that receive funding from a church or religious organization, and keeps close ties to that organization.

  • Curriculum includes general religious education in addition to secular subjects
  • Open to all children in the parish
  • Functions as a quasi-public school, paralleling state-run institutions

Parochial schools have been built and centered around a wide range of religious beliefs, with some of the most popular being Catholic and Christian. That said, there are also Jewish and Muslim schools that meet the criteria of Parochial schools, despite not using that term due to its historical association with Christian parishes.

It's also important to note that not all religious schools are Parochial schools. For example, a Catholic school is not a Parochial school if it receives its funding from a source other than the church.

Parochial schools are also a favorite of conservative Mennonites, the Amish, and Old Order Mennonites.

--

Boarding schools need no introduction. To be considered a boarding school, it must offer food and lodging to its students. Boarding schools are private, and use different methodologies depending on the institution, but common themes might include:

  • Requiring students to live on campus
  • Encouraging students to participate in on-site extracurricular activities
  • Families of staff residing on campus, serving in coaching or advising roles
